one_liner: LMDB fork: embedded memory-mapped ACID B+tree KV store; author reports 10-30% faster in-tmpfs CRUD than LMDB.
what_it_does: An embedded, transactional, ordered key-value store (maps plus sorted multimaps, many named tables per file) kept in one memory-mapped file that many threads and processes on the same host can read and update with full ACID guarantees, with no server and no internal threads. It forked from LMDB in 2015 and keeps LMDB's env/txn/dbi/cursor C API model under mdbx_ names (the author describes the API as 'mostly the same'), and it adds a C++ API (mdbx.h++) that throws exceptions and uses std::pmr allocators when available. Moving from LMDB means renaming calls and reviewing changed semantics, not relinking.
how_it_is_fast: The core is LMDB's design: a copy-on-write (shadow-paging) B+tree in a memory-mapped file with MVCC snapshots, so reads are zero-copy pointer walks with no buffer pool and no WAL, and readers are wait-free without atomic operations. On top of that libmdbx adds LIFO reuse of freed pages (shorter page circulation, better write-back cache hit rates), 'refund' auto-compaction that truncates freed tail pages at commit, 'Big Foot' chunking of huge retired-page lists, bulk deletion by cutting whole B-tree branches, and mdbx_cache_get, which stores a key's version and mmap offset client-side and stops the B-tree descent at the first page that has not changed. The top '30% faster' figure needs builds that relax runtime checks (the MDBX_DISABLE_VALIDATION option, described as bringing corruption detection 'closer to the LMDB').
when_to_use: Read-dominated embedded workloads that need ACID transactions, sorted keys and range scans, where readers must never block the single writer and read throughput should scale across cores.
Several processes on one host sharing a single database file without running a database server.

You already run LMDB and hit its limits: keys longer than 511 bytes (libmdbx allows 2022 bytes at 4 KiB pages, 32742 at 64 KiB), a data file that never shrinks, bloat from slow readers, or corruption after crashes in no-sync modes (MDBX_SAFE_NOSYNC keeps the DB consistent).
Hot point lookups on keys that rarely change, where mdbx_cache_get can skip most of the B-tree descent.
Bulk loading pre-sorted data with the append operation on Linux, the platform the author recommends for speed; Ethereum clients (Erigon, Reth, Silkworm) use it in production.
when_not_to_use: Write-heavy workloads with strict durability: only one write transaction runs at a time and the README says syncing shadow pages to disk can bottleneck write-intensive loads. The write-optimized LSM engines in this category are a better fit.

Performance-sensitive Windows or macOS deployments: by default Windows uses LockFileEx and macOS/iOS use F_FULLFSYNC, and the README says both make libmdbx slower than LMDB. WSL1 is refused outright (ENOLCK) and shrinking the file on Windows is limited.

Long-running read transactions (analytics scans, backups by iteration) alongside steady writes: pinned pages make the file grow and throughput drop unless you use transaction parking or the Handle-Slow-Readers callback.

You need a current head-to-head against LMDB: the 10-30% figures are old first-party claims (an 'up to 20% faster' version was posted in 2019) and have not been republished against LMDB 1.0, which shipped in July 2026 with faster large-transaction commits.

Processes that open untrusted or corrupted database files, or strict supply-chain policies: 2026 fuzzing found an out-of-bounds read in mdbx_env_chk (issue #375) and a null dereference on corrupted DBs (#297), both since fixed. The project is still 0.x and led by one author after corporate funding ended in 2025, and the README says the successor MithrilDB may be withheld from countries that sanction Russia.

integration.form: source-drop (amalgamated mdbx.c + mdbx.h, optional mdbx.c++ + mdbx.h++); CMake or GNU Make builds it as a static or shared lib
integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and pthreads (ntdll.lib on Windows); bash, GNU Make or CMake to build
integration.min_toolchain: C99/C11 (CMake picks C23, C11 or C99; GNU Make uses -std=gnu11); C++ API needs C++11 and prefers C++17 to C++23. Tested since 2026 with GCC 11.3+, Clang 14+, MSVC 19.44+ (VS 2022), Elbrus LCC 1.28+; MinGW 10.2+ on Windows
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows (not WSL1), macOS, iOS, Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, DragonFly, Solaris/illumos, HarmonyOS and other POSIX.1-2008 systems; the file format depends on endianness only, not 32/64-bit; the header prints a warning when built for RISC-V
integration.thread_safety: One environment can be shared by threads and processes. Writers are serialized by a single mutex (one write transaction at a time), and readers never block writers or each other. A transaction or cursor must never be used from two threads at once. Read transactions are tied to their OS thread unless MDBX_NOSTICKYTHREADS is set (meant for Go/Rust runtimes). A write transaction must commit or abort on the thread that began it. Do not reuse an env in a child after fork() (use mdbx_env_resurrect_after_fork) and do not open the same DB twice in one process.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the C API keeps LMDB's model and error-code range under mdbx_ names, but it is not ABI-compatible and no LMDB file-format compatibility is documented (an LMDB-to-MDBX migration guide is still on the TODO list). Some semantics differ: every cursor must be closed explicitly, ambiguous updates return MDBX_EMULTIVAL, and fsync/locking defaults differ on macOS and Windows.

gotchas: Values returned by get/cursor calls point into the map and stay valid only until the next update or the end of the transaction. Writing through them causes SIGSEGV, or silent DB corruption under MDBX_WRITEMAP or on dirty pages.

mdbx_dbi_close is not synchronized with transactions running on other threads. Nested-transaction DDL had data-loss and assertion bugs fixed in mid-2026: a drop inside a child transaction that was then aborted emptied the table (#361), and rename caused a commit assertion (#360). Pin to the stable branch or a release.
Sharing a DB across containers requires one kernel page cache, a shared PID namespace (e.g. --pid=host) and matching libmdbx/libc build options (compare the 'options:' line of mdbx_chk -V).
Since December 2025 only amalgamated source ships and most tests are not included, so you cannot rerun the full test suite from a release tarball.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: SplinterDB, NuDB, TerarkDB and Titan are all write-optimized engines benchmarked against RocksDB on insert and load throughput (for example SplinterDB reports 6-10x faster inserts and Titan about 70% faster loading). Pick libmdbx when the workload is read-dominated, needs ordered range scans with zero-copy reads and snapshot isolation, or has several processes sharing one file. Pick a sibling when ingest rate is the bottleneck.
verified_claims_summary: All numbers are first-party: the README says in-tmpfs CRUD runs of the ioArena harness show libmdbx 10-20% faster than LMDB, and up to 30% faster in builds that drop runtime checks. It publishes no result tables, hardware, compiler flags or LMDB version. The repo's make bench targets default to 25M operations in nosync mode with 4 reader threads for get/iterate, on upstream ioArena's defaults of 16-byte keys and 32-byte values. The '10-100K times faster' line names no cases; separately, the author claims mdbx_cache_get speeds up get by 'several tens of thousands of times'.
status_note: Actively maintained: stable v0.14.4 shipped 2026-09-19, master is v0.15 development, and the last commit was 2026-09-25. It is Apache-2.0 amalgamated C and easy to vendor, but still pre-1.0, driven by one lead author, and developed on SourceCraft with GitHub (Mithril-mine) only as a mirror.
